advantages: Tamper-evidence is structural, not promised: editing any old block changes its hash and breaks every subsequent prevHash, so the tampering is visible without any central log.
The header is a compact summary, so a node can check a block's identity and its transaction set from a fixed-size header plus a Merkle proof.
Every node can verify independently, which is what removes the need to trust whoever holds the ledger.
The same structure gives efficient light clients: a Merkle root in the header plus a short proof replaces downloading the whole block.
limitations: The chain link only detects tampering, it does not prevent it; a rewrite of history is still physically possible, it just requires redoing all the work.
A singly linked list is not random-access - finding block 1000000 needs an index or a full scan, unlike a flat table.
The hash of the whole history gives no fine-grained accounting: you cannot ask 'what changed at block k' without the intermediate data.
Every full node stores and re-executes the whole chain, so storage and validation cost grow linearly with history.
Storing the transactions in a fixed order inside the block is a design choice that some newer chains (EIP-1559, blobs) have had to bend to cut fees.
Data structures for Blockchain.memoryTrick: **Header links blocks, Merkle root links transactions - pull one page and every page after it is wrong.**

examAnswer.question: Describe the main data structures used in a blockchain and explain why a linked list of hashes is used instead of a flat table. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**The structures.** A blockchain's ledger is a singly linked list of blocks. Each block has a fixed-size header and a payload. The header holds five things: the previous block's hash, the Merkle root of the block's transactions, a timestamp, a nonce and the consensus target. The payload is the ordered list of transactions, which are themselves hashed pairwise into a Merkle tree whose root is the only thing the header needs to store.

**Why not a flat table.** A flat table is a list of rows. Nothing inside it says that row 40 was written before row 41 or that row 40 has not since been edited. A row can be changed in place and the table still looks perfectly valid - the change is invisible unless somebody keeps a separate copy of the old contents to compare against, which is exactly the trust problem a blockchain exists to remove. The linked list removes the need for that comparison copy. Because block k's header contains the hash of block k-1, and block k's own hash covers its header, editing block k changes its hash; that hash was stored in block k+1's prevHash field, so block k+1 now points at the wrong predecessor; that breaks block k+2, and the cascade runs all the way to the tip. One edit to one old row turns into a chain of mismatched fingerprints from that point forward.

**The consequence.** Tampering is not prevented - history can still be rewritten, it just requires redoing all the downstream work. What changes is the burden: detection no longer depends on trusting any single copy of the ledger, because every node recomputes the links itself and any divergence is obvious. The Merkle root completes the same job one level down, committing to every transaction in the block without listing them, so the header stays fixed-size no matter how many transactions the block holds, and a light client can verify one transaction from a short proof instead of taking the whole block on trust.

advantages: One 32-byte root commits to the whole transaction set, so the block header can be verified without holding the payloads.
Inclusion proofs are logarithmic: a 1,024-leaf tree needs a 10-level path, so a light client proves one transaction with about 10 hashes instead of 1,024 leaves.
Tampering is localised - a changed transaction changes one path up to the root, so the mismatch identifies the culprit leaf.
The verifier does almost no work: re-hashing up one path is a handful of hashes, so the proof can be checked on a phone.
The same construction scales to state proofs, where it is how Ethereum proves one account's balance without downloading the whole state trie.
limitations: A maliciously constructed tree with duplicated leaves can pass an old SPV client that checks only that a leaf appears in the path, so modern clients must also check that the proof has the expected number of distinct hashes.
Building the tree is O(n) hashing work, so it is real cost on the producing node rather than free.
The tree commits to the set of leaves but not to their order unless the order is fixed by construction - order has to be agreed separately.
Odd numbers of leaves need a defined rule (duplicate the last, or promote it), and different chains make different choices, which is a portability trap.
The tree says nothing about the validity of a transaction - it proves the transaction is in the block, not that it was legitimate.
Merkle Trees.memoryTrick: **Hash up in pairs, proof goes up one path - n leaves give n-1 internal nodes and ceil(log2 n) proof length.**

examAnswer.question: Build a Merkle tree for four transactions, show how an inclusion proof for one transaction works, and state the number of hash nodes per level and the proof length. (15 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Definition.** A Merkle tree is a binary hash tree. Each leaf is hashed, and the resulting hashes are hashed in pairs, and those results are hashed in pairs again, and so on until exactly one hash remains. That last hash, the root, is a single fingerprint committing to every leaf in the tree. In a blockchain the root is stored in the block header, so the header commits to every transaction in the block without listing any of them.

**Building it level by level, with four transactions A, B, C, D.**
Level 0 - the leaves: hash each transaction individually. That gives 4 leaf hashes: H(A), H(B), H(C), H(D). No hashing has combined anything yet; these are just fingerprints of the four payloads.
Level 1 - the first combination: hash adjacent pairs. H(A|B) and H(C|D). That is 2 hashes, and 2 internal nodes so far. The total number of hash nodes at this level is 2, exactly half the leaves.
Level 2 - the root: hash the two level-1 nodes together, H(H(A|B) | H(C|D)). That is 1 hash and the 3rd internal node. The tree now has 4 leaf hashes plus 3 internal hashes, 7 hash nodes in total, and the number of hashing levels above the leaves is 2.

**The counting rule.** For a tree with n leaves there are always n-1 internal nodes, because every internal node is the join of exactly two children. 4 leaves give 3 internal nodes; 3 leaves give 2 internal nodes; 1,024 leaves give 1,023 internal nodes. The number of hashing levels is ceil(log2 n): 2 for 4 leaves, 2 for 3 leaves, 10 for 1,024 leaves.

**Proving inclusion.** To prove that leaf A is in the tree, the prover supplies only the sibling hash at each level on A's path - not the other leaves. For our 4-leaf tree that proof is exactly two hashes: H(B) and H(C|D). The verifier then works upward: it computes H(A | H(B)), then computes H(that | H(C|D)), and checks that the result equals the root in the block header. If it matches, A is in the block; if any leaf or any sibling hash was altered, the recomputed value differs from the root and the proof fails. The proof length is the number of levels on the path, ceil(log2 n), so a 1,024-leaf tree needs a 10-hash proof. In the odd-leaf case, a 3-leaf tree has 2 internal nodes and 2 hash levels, and the proof for leaf C is the single sibling hash H(A|B), because the root is then H(H(A|B) | C) and can be recomputed from that one hash.

**Consequence.** This is what makes a light client viable: a phone can prove one transaction is in a block using about log2(n) hashes and a header it already trusts, instead of downloading the whole block or the whole chain. It is also why a Merkle root is a good tamper detector - altering any single transaction changes one path up to the tree and therefore changes the root, so the mismatch points straight at the altered leaf.

advantages: Public on-chain data is verifiable by anyone without any trust in the operator, which is exactly what makes it useful as an audit record.
Permissioned on-chain data keeps a single, shared, tamper-evident source of truth while controlling who may read and who may write.
The hash-anchor pattern keeps the confidentiality of off-chain data and the integrity of the ledger at the same time, so nothing is lost by moving the data out.
Key-based access control allows revocation and per-party selective disclosure without rewriting history.
limitations: A public ledger stores everything forever at full redundancy - it is the wrong place for large or frequently changing data.
Hash anchoring proves integrity but not authorship or freshness: it cannot prove that a document existed before a certain time unless a trusted timestamp is involved.
Encryption with a shared key means whoever holds the key can decrypt everything, so key management becomes the real risk, and a compromised key cannot be un-issued.
Permissioned chains shrink the trust surface but also the node count, which weakens the economic security that makes public chains safe.
The right-to-erasure conflict cannot be solved on-chain at all - deleting a record from an immutable ledger is impossible, so compliance has to be met off-chain.
Shared data.memoryTrick: **Three drawers: glass for anyone, a door for members, a locked office off-chain with only the hash on the wall.**

examAnswer.question: Distinguish public, permissioned and private shared data in a blockchain and explain how private data stays confidential without losing tamper-evidence. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Public shared data.** Written on-chain in the clear and readable by any node in the network. This is where public keys, transaction hashes, public announcements and audit records belong. Its value is precisely that it is verifiable by everyone without trusting whoever operates the network - which also means it must never carry personal or commercially sensitive content, because it is readable forever and cannot be deleted.

**Permissioned shared data.** Also written on-chain, so it keeps the shared, tamper-evident properties, but access is restricted by identity: only admitted network members may read it and only certified organisations may write it. Because the membership is controlled, this is where commercially sensitive content can safely be recorded - a consortium ledger, for example, where each participant's records are visible to the other participants and to nobody else.

**Private data.** Belongs to one organisation and stays off the ledger entirely, in the owner's own storage. What goes on-chain is only a hash of the off-chain document - a commitment, not the content. To serve the authorised parties, the owner publishes the pre-image, which they hash and compare against the recorded commitment.

**How confidentiality and tamper-evidence coexist.** The on-chain hash is an anchor. If anyone alters the off-chain copy, the recomputed hash no longer equals the recorded one, and the tampering is detectable by anyone who checks. The content stays private because the hash is not reversible into the document, and access to the document is controlled by encryption: encrypt before storing off-chain, keep the key under access control, and put only the commitment on-chain.

**The consequence to state.** The right-to-erasure problem is the one regulators care about, and it can only be solved by keeping the personal data off-chain - encrypt it, revoke access by rotating the key, and leave only a hash behind. An immutable ledger cannot forget, so anything that must be forgotten must never be written to it in the first place.

advantages: Separating the layers lets you replace the gossip mechanism or the consensus engine without rewriting the applications above.
Each layer has its own failure mode, so a symptom points straight at the layer that is broken instead of at the whole system.
Standardising the transport underneath means many networks can be built on the same networking stack.
limitations: The separation is conceptual - a real implementation always leaks some coupling between the layers, especially around transaction validity.
The middle layer is the slowest to change: consensus is baked into the state machine, so swapping it is a fork.
Gossip protocols are hard to tune: the choice between flooding and pull-based propagation trades bandwidth against latency, and both ends of the range are bad for someone.
Debugging still crosses layers, since a stuck transaction can be a gossip failure, a consensus stall or a bad application contract.
Protocols.memoryTrick: **Application says what, consensus says which order, gossip says how it travels.**

examAnswer.question: Explain the three protocol layers in a blockchain, what each is responsible for, and the benefit of separating them. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Three layers, three jobs.** The application-facing protocol at the top defines what a transaction means: the transaction format, the wallet that signs it, the RPC calls an application makes to read state and submit transactions. The consensus protocol in the middle defines which ordering of blocks is valid: given a set of candidate blocks it produces one canonical chain and settles on it, whether by proof of stake, by a voting service or by a notary panel. The gossip and broadcast protocol at the bottom defines how blocks and transactions reach the other peers at all: it propagates them over TCP/IP, and it is what a private relay or an alternative transport would replace. Below that sits transport itself, which is the least interesting layer.

**Why the split matters.** Each layer fails in its own way, and separating them is what lets a symptom be diagnosed. A transaction that is malformed or that reverts is an application-layer fault. Two competing chains, or a chain that simply stops advancing, is a consensus fault. Transactions that never propagate, or blocks that never arrive at some node, are a gossip fault - a partitioned network. If the layers were one design, these three failures would look identical from the outside.

**The second benefit.** Because the layers are separable, the gossip layer or the consensus engine can be replaced without rewriting the applications on top. A chain can adopt a different broadcast mechanism, or move from one consensus mechanism to another, while the applications, wallets and contracts continue to work against the same interface. This is the concrete form of the fat-versus-thin distinction in the next topic: what makes the layers separable is that the rules and state live in the protocol layer rather than being smeared across the application layer.

advantages: Value capture moves to the protocol layer: fees, staking rewards and MEV accrue to the platform rather than leaking to an application built on top of it.
The protocol can enforce rules itself, rejecting a message that violates them instead of passing it on - which is what removes the trusted intermediary.
Rules and state sitting together in one system means the guarantee is enforced by consensus and is therefore as strong as the chain's security.
Composability: because the rules are code at the protocol layer, other contracts and applications can build on them, so the network gets more useful as it grows.
limitations: Rigidity: the rules are baked into the state machine, so changing them is a governance decision and often a hard fork, whereas a thin protocol can evolve without breaking its users.
Upgrades become political - a rule change needs agreement from validators, node operators and users, not just a code push.
The protocol layer accumulates the bugs of every application rule placed on it, and a bug there is much harder to escape than a bug in a normal program.
Fatness can crowd out usability: the protocol grows heavy weights, MEV extraction and fee markets that a thin protocol simply never had to face.
A fat protocol also concentrates regulatory attention, because the rules it enforces are now the platform's own legal position.
Fat Protocols.memoryTrick: **Thin carries, fat carries the rules - smart contracts are the hinge that makes the protocol the enforcer.**

examAnswer.question: Distinguish thin and fat protocols, state where the rules live in each, and explain why smart contracts make a protocol fat. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Thin protocols.** A thin protocol defines only the message format and the transport, and leaves every rule to the application above it. TCP moves bytes and HTTP moves requests; neither knows anything about what the bytes mean, and both accept whatever is well-formed at their layer. The application enforces its own business rules, and the value created by those rules is captured at the application layer - the protocol is interchangeable infrastructure that anyone can copy.

**Fat protocols.** A fat protocol carries not only messages but also the rules and the state those rules govern, so the protocol itself is the enforcement mechanism. The classic example is Ethereum: the transaction format, the state transition function and the rules of every deployed contract all sit inside the protocol, and a transaction that violates a rule is rejected by the protocol rather than passed on to be policed by some application server.

**Smart contracts are the hinge.** The move that makes a protocol fat is putting business logic on-chain. Once the rules and the state they act on are inside the protocol, the protocol stops being a dumb pipe and becomes the place where behaviour is decided and enforced. That single change has two knock-on effects. Value capture moves up a layer: fees, staking rewards and MEV accrue to the protocol, because that is where the rules and the economics now live. And the rules become the protocol's own state machine, which makes them correspondingly hard to change.

**The trade-off to state.** Fat protocols are harder to evolve. In a thin protocol, changing the application changes nothing for anybody else. In a fat protocol, the rules are baked into the consensus state machine, so changing them is a governance decision and usually a hard fork - every node must agree, and the community must agree. Fat protocols therefore capture more value at the protocol layer, and they pay for it with rigidity and with the platform inheriting the responsibility for every rule written on it.

advantages: Ethereum gives an open developer ecosystem, thousands of integrations and a large liquid market for the assets it secures.
Fabric gives certified identity, private channels, pluggable consensus and deterministic finality - exactly what a consortium of businesses needs.
Corda's notary model removes unnecessary consensus from bilateral contracts, so they settle quickly without a global ordering.
Quorum gives an institution Ethereum tooling and EVM contracts without inheriting public-network anonymity or open participation.
limitations: Public chains give probabilistic finality and unpredictable fees, which many regulated businesses cannot accept.
Permissioned chains have a small validator set, so their security comes from the membership agreement rather than from economic stake, and they are not censorship-resistant.
Corda's notary model and selective distribution weaken the shared global state, so cross-network interoperability is harder.
Every platform choice is a lock-in: contracts written for one EVM dialect or one identity system are costly to move.
Enterprise platforms cost real money - membership, certificate authority, operations - so 'permissioned is free' is never true.
Platforms.memoryTrick: **Three questions settle any platform: who may write, how do nodes agree, when is it final.**

examAnswer.question: Compare Ethereum, Hyperledger Fabric, Corda and Quorum as blockchain platforms in terms of identity model, consensus and finality. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Three axes decide everything.** Any platform is a choice of three things: who is allowed to write and read (permissioning), how nodes agree on the order of blocks (consensus), and how finality arrives - probabilistically, as confidence that grows, or deterministically, as certainty on a stated condition. Answer in those three columns and most exam questions on platforms are done.

**Ethereum.** Public: anyone can submit a transaction, no admission control. Consensus is proof of stake with a large, slashed validator set. Finality is probabilistic - a transaction is exponentially more likely final as confirmations accumulate, and the protocol's finality gadgets settle it formally. You buy openness and ecosystem size; you pay in unpredictable fees and in the fact that finality is a probability rather than a guarantee.

**Hyperledger Fabric.** Permissioned: participants are admitted, and each organisation gets a certified identity, which is what makes private channels possible - data shared between a subset of members without being visible to the rest of the network. Consensus is pluggable, chosen to suit the membership and the threat model. Finality is deterministic once the ordering service commits. You buy privacy, identity and predictable latency; you pay in a smaller, less open network whose security rests on the membership agreement.

**Corda.** Permissioned, and designed around a notary model: a small set of notaries order transactions, so a bilateral contract between two known parties does not require global consensus and settles quickly. Finality is immediate once the notary commits. It is the natural choice for bilateral and multi-party commercial contracts; the cost is that there is no single global shared state across separate Corda networks.

**Quorum.** A permissioned fork of Ethereum used by financial consortia - CLs Bank being the well-known case - so members keep Ethereum tooling, the EVM and Solidity while running a private, governed network.

**The business conclusion.** The choice is openness against control. A public chain buys you a large developer ecosystem and open access; a permissioned chain buys you certified identity, privacy and deterministic finality. For regulated data, bilateral contracts or consortium processes, permissioned wins; for open, incentive-driven applications, Ethereum wins.

advantages: The user keeps custody: the wallet holds the key, so no operator can move the user's funds, which is what makes the application genuinely decentralised rather than merely distributed.
Each part is separately monetisable - hosting, indexer services, oracle feeds and contract deployment are all revenue lines without needing to own the assets.
The rules are public and auditable, so a business can promise its users a specific behaviour and have that promise verifiable.
Composable: a dApp can call other contracts, so new applications are assembled rather than rebuilt.
limitations: A hosted node provider re-introduces the trusted intermediary the architecture was meant to remove, so the decentralisation claim is only as good as the provider mix.
The UX cost is real: every action is a signed transaction with a gas fee and a wait, which is why most dApps lose users at the first payment.
The oracle is a single point of truth the chain cannot check, so a wrong price feeds a correct contract to a wrong conclusion.
The front end can still be taken down, censored or swapped by the operator, so the interface is not decentralised even when the contract is.
Gas volatility makes pricing and unit economics unstable, and a popular dApp can price its own users out.
DAPPS.memoryTrick: **Five parts: front end, wallet, node, contract, oracle - the wallet is the one that must not belong to the operator.**

examAnswer.question: Describe the anatomy of a decentralised application and explain how its parts map onto the business models of the unit. (5 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**Five parts.** A dApp is assembled from five pieces. The front end is what the user sees and clicks - a web or mobile interface that builds transaction objects and reads state. The wallet holds the user's private key and signs every transaction. The node or provider supplies chain data and submits transactions to the network. The smart contract holds the rules and the state and lives at an address that is the application's on-chain identity. The oracle supplies real-world facts that the chain itself cannot know.

**Why the wallet is the decisive part.** The user signs with their own key, so the dApp never takes custody of funds or authority. That single fact is what separates a decentralised application from a merely distributed one - a web app with a blockchain API still keeps the keys server-side and is custodial no matter how it is deployed. Everything else in the stack can be centralised without changing that verdict, but if the operator holds the key, the decentralisation claim is false.

**Where the other parts sit.** The front end holds no keys and no trust, but it can still be censored or taken offline, which is a known weakness. A full node verifies for itself; a hosted provider such as an Infura-style endpoint is a convenience that quietly re-introduces a trusted intermediary, so a serious deployment mixes both. The contract is where the rules and the state live and where the guarantee is real, because consensus enforces it. The oracle is an external input: contracts only see on-chain data, so a correct contract given a wrong price still produces a wrong result.

**The business mapping.** Each of the five parts is a separate product and therefore a separate revenue line: the front end can be paid for or ad-supported, the provider can charge for hosted access and indexed data, the contract can carry deployment and interaction fees, and the oracle can be sold as a data feed. This is where the Unit 5 business models attach to the technical stack - a dApp can sell subscriptions at the front end, charge for infrastructure, take a cut of the contract's economics, or sell the oracle feed itself. The same five-part anatomy is the restaurant analogy: the waiter, the customer's own money, the kitchen, the recipe and the delivery van.

advantages: Execution is deterministic and audited by the protocol, so no intermediary has to be trusted to honour the agreement.
State changes are recorded in the shared ledger, so all parties see the same history with no reconciliation step.
Gas bounds execution, so a contract cannot loop forever or exhaust the chain - the classic denial-of-service vector is designed out.
Events give off-chain applications a cheap way to follow state changes without reading the whole ledger, which is what makes the dApp layer practical.
Composability lets one contract call another, so agreements can be assembled into complex business processes.
limitations: The deployed code is immutable, so a bug cannot be patched in place; the usual workarounds - a proxy or a migration to a new contract - add their own risk and complexity.
A revert still burns the gas it used, so a badly written function can be made expensive to fail deliberately.
Storage is the dominant cost: a new 32-byte word costs 20,000 gas against 21,000 for a whole ETH transfer, so contracts are forced to be frugal with data.
All on-chain logic is public, so any secret embedded in a contract is readable by everyone, including the private keys that should never have been there.
The contract sees only on-chain data, so it needs a trusted oracle and inherits that trust.
Determinism is a constraint as well as a guarantee: the code cannot depend on wall-clock time, randomness or any external call without losing reproducibility.
Smart Contracts.memoryTrick: **Deploy once, run on every copy, gas prices the work, events tell the app, code is frozen but state moves.**

examAnswer.question: Explain the deploy-and-execute semantics of a smart contract, the difference between immutable code and mutable state, and the role of gas, events and access control. (15 marks)
examAnswer.full:
**What it is.** A smart contract is code deployed to an address on the ledger. When a transaction satisfies the conditions the code checks, the contract executes deterministically and its state changes become part of the shared record. The analogy is a vending machine: the rules are locked behind the glass, you put in the coin and press the button, and the outcome is dispensed with nobody supervising it.

**Deploy.** The compiled bytecode plus constructor arguments are sent as a transaction. The constructor runs exactly once, setting up initial state, and the resulting code and storage are fixed at a new address. From this point the contract has an identity on the network: it holds a balance, it has a nonce, it can be called, and it can be the destination of a transfer like any other account.

**Execute.** A transaction or a message targets the address with a function selector and arguments. Every node runs the same code against its own copy of the state, and because the execution is deterministic, every node independently arrives at the same result. Each call either succeeds and commits its state changes, or it reverts, in which case all state changes are rolled back and the call fails. The state changes that do succeed are written into the block, the block's Merkle root changes with them, and the shared record is updated.

**Code is immutable, state is mutable.** This is the distinction the question is built on. Once deployed, the code cannot be edited in place: it is fixed at the address, so a bug in the logic cannot be patched the way an ordinary program can be patched. The state the contract manages is completely mutable - balances, counters, ownership records and mappings all change transaction by transaction. So the data can be corrected and the rules cannot. The standard remedies are a proxy contract, where the deployed contract delegates to an implementation that can be repointed, or migrating to a fresh contract and moving the state across; both add complexity, and neither is the same as editing code in place.

**Gas.** Every operation is metered and priced in gas, which is what makes execution bounded: a contract cannot loop forever and freeze the chain, and the cost of an operation is proportional to the work it does. Storage is far more expensive than computation - storing a new 32-byte word costs 20,000 gas, while a plain ETH transfer costs 21,000 gas for the whole call. At a typical 20 gwei, a transfer costs 21,000 x 20 x 10^-9 ETH, about 0.00042 ETH. Against the classic 30-million-gas block limit that leaves room for roughly 1,400 simple transfers per block. A reverted call still consumes the gas it burned; only the unused remainder is refunded, which is why a deliberately failing function can be made expensive to trigger.

**Events.** The contract emits events, which are written to the transaction log with a topic and indexed data. They are how off-chain applications follow the chain: the front end subscribes to the logs instead of polling the whole state, so it learns of a change without scanning the ledger. Events are not stored in the contract's storage variables and cannot be read back by the contract itself.

**Access control.** Which caller may invoke which function is decided in the code, usually with owner and role checks in modifiers. This is where the authorisation model of the application lives - only the owner may pause a contract, only the registrar may add a user, only a specific role may issue. Combined with the immutable code, this is what stops the contract from being an open door to state that the business intended to keep closed.

**The consequence.** The contract's guarantees are only as strong as the assumptions in its code, and the code cannot be changed. That is the trade the whole architecture makes: execution is guaranteed, and the rules are fixed.
